claims.text: The proposed intervention is to add approximately 3–4 at.% Hf to nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11.
Adding 3–4 at.% Hf will suppress irradiation-induced Cr-V-rich precipitate formation near 8 dpa.
The Hf-modified alloy will preserve the baseline alloy's low irradiation hardening and radiation resistance.
A 3–4 at.% Hf addition will retain practical bulk manufacturability.
The initial W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy is nanocrystalline and produced by severe plastic deformation methods such as cold rolling or wire drawing.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 develops Cr-V-rich precipitates under energetic-particle irradiation at around 8 dpa.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits low irradiation hardening and acceptable radiation resistance.
At approximately 500°C, irradiation-induced defects will have sufficient mobility to permit recovery.
A specimen temperature of approximately 500°C is low enough to limit diffusion-driven precipitation.
Hf atoms will preferentially segregate to grain boundaries and irradiation-defect sinks.
Hf segregation will alter local diffusion kinetics and reduce the mobility of Cr and V.
Reduced Cr and V mobility will minimize the nucleation and growth of Cr-V-rich precipitates during irradiation.
Hf modifies solute interactions and defect-sink efficiencies in the irradiated alloy.

After irradiation to 8 dpa at approximately 500°C, the Hf-modified alloy will have a lower density or smaller size of Cr-V-rich precipitates, or a delayed precipitation onset, relative to the unmodified alloy.
The proposed suppression effect is expected to hold up to approximately 8 dpa and around 500°C.
At higher temperatures, enhanced solute diffusion may overcome the proposed Hf suppression effect.
At doses substantially above 8 dpa, other damage mechanisms may become important.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis requires precipitate suppression while preserving low hardening, but the falsification rule requires both failure to reduce precipitates and absence of improved hardening. Hardening improvement is not required by the hypothesis, and failure of precipitate suppression alone should be sufficient to reject its central claim.
